readAloud.text: More than half a million pieces of debris now orbit the Earth, travelling at speeds that make even a paint fragment capable of disabling a satellite. This cloud of defunct spacecraft, spent rocket stages and collision fragments threatens the communications and navigation systems on which modern life depends. Space agencies are therefore developing tracking networks and testing technologies to capture and remove the most dangerous objects.

The concept of lifelong learning holds that education does not end with graduation but continues throughout a person's career and beyond. As automation transforms the labour market, workers must repeatedly update their skills to remain employable. Governments and employers are responding with short courses, flexible qualifications and paid study leave, while universities are redesigning programmes so that adults can return to study without interrupting their working lives.

Laboratories can now produce diamonds that are chemically and visually identical to stones mined from the earth. Created in a matter of weeks rather than over billions of years, these gems cost considerably less and avoid the environmental damage associated with large-scale mining. Nevertheless, the traditional diamond industry argues that only natural stones carry the rarity and romance that make a diamond truly precious.

Seaweed farming is among the fastest-growing sectors of global aquaculture, requiring no fertiliser, no fresh water and no land. The plants absorb carbon dioxide and excess nutrients as they grow, improving water quality around the farms. Beyond its use in food, seaweed now appears in cosmetics, animal feed, biodegradable packaging and fertilisers, and researchers are investigating whether large-scale cultivation could meaningfully reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Crows and their relatives possess cognitive abilities that rival those of great apes, despite having brains the size of a walnut. In experiments, they have bent wire into hooks to retrieve food, planned for future events, and recognised individual human faces years after a single encounter. Neuroscientists have discovered that a densely packed region of the crow brain performs functions comparable to the mammalian prefrontal cortex.

Dark sky reserves are protected areas where artificial lighting is strictly controlled so that the night sky remains visible in its natural state. To gain official status, communities must demonstrate exceptional starry nights and commit to responsible outdoor lighting. Astronomers value these sanctuaries for research, while ecologists note that darkness is essential for migrating birds, nocturnal insects and many other species harmed by light pollution.

Micro-credentials are short, focused qualifications that certify mastery of a specific skill, from data analysis to project management. Unlike traditional degrees, they can be completed in weeks and stacked towards larger qualifications over time. Supporters argue they make education more responsive to a rapidly changing job market, while critics warn that the lack of common standards leaves employers uncertain about what each credential actually guarantees.

describeImage.title: Sources of tracked space debris in Earth orbit
describeImage.sample: The pie chart illustrates the sources of tracked space debris in Earth orbit. Fragmentation debris from collisions and explosions forms the largest category, at forty percent. Defunct satellites account for thirty percent, followed by spent rocket bodies at seventeen percent. Mission-related objects, such as lens caps and tools, make up the remaining thirteen percent. In conclusion, most orbital debris comes from break-up events and dead satellites.

retellLecture.title: Returning museum objects to their countries of origin
retellLecture.sample: The lecture discussed the growing debate over returning cultural objects held in Western museums to their countries of origin. The speaker explained that many items were taken during the colonial era under circumstances now considered unacceptable. Some museums favour repatriation or long-term loans, while others argue that universal museums protect fragile artefacts and allow global audiences to compare cultures. The speaker concluded that curators are increasingly choosing partnership, shared ownership and rotating exhibitions instead of outright possession.
retellLecture.text: Museums in Europe and North America hold millions of objects acquired during the colonial era, often under circumstances that would be unacceptable today. In recent years, source countries have pressed for the return of significant items, from sacred statues to royal treasures. Some institutions have responded positively, arguing that objects carry their deepest meaning in their place of origin and that long-term loans can preserve access for international audiences. Others resist, claiming that universal museums protect fragile artefacts from conflict and allow global visitors to compare cultures. Increasingly, however, curators are choosing partnership over possession, agreeing to share ownership, fund conservation abroad, and rotate exhibitions between continents.

retellLecture.title: How climate change is reshaping insurance
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained how the insurance industry is responding to climate change. The speaker said that more frequent floods, wildfires and storms have produced record payouts and sharply rising premiums, and that private insurers have withdrawn entirely from some coastal districts. To manage the danger, insurers are investing in sophisticated climate models and rewarding customers who strengthen their properties. Finally, the speaker noted that when premiums become unaffordable, they signal which places may soon be too risky to inhabit.
retellLecture.text: Insurance companies are among the first businesses to feel the financial impact of climate change. As floods, wildfires and storms become more frequent, insurers pay out record sums, and premiums in high-risk regions are rising sharply. In some coastal districts, private insurers have withdrawn entirely, leaving governments to act as insurers of last resort. To manage the danger, the industry is investing in sophisticated climate models and rewarding customers who strengthen their properties against extreme weather. Some experts argue that insurance pricing sends a powerful signal: when premiums become unaffordable, they reveal which places may soon be too risky to inhabit at all.

respondToSituation.sample: Hi, this is Jamie Collins from flat 4B, Maple Court. My heating stopped working two days ago, and I've already sent two emails without any response. I'd also appreciate a quick written update by email so I know something is actually happening. Thanks very much for your help.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Are micro-credentials a worthwhile alternative to a traditional degree?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The speakers debated whether micro-credentials can replace a traditional degree. Speaker A praised them as fast, affordable and increasingly respected by major companies. Speaker B was sceptical, noting that employers still filter CVs by degree and that there are no agreed standards, so proper accreditation would be needed. Speaker C took a middle position, arguing that micro-credentials are ideal for mid-career reskilling but that young students gain broader benefits such as networks and maturity from university. Overall, the group agreed micro-credentials are valuable supplements rather than full replacements.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, I think they're brilliant. Not everyone can afford three or four years at university. With micro-credentials you can learn a specific skill, like data analysis, in a few weeks and prove it to an employer straight away.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd be cautious. Most employers I know still filter CVs by degree. And almost anyone can set up an online badge — there's no agreed standard, so how do you know whether the course was any good?

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's changing, though. Big technology firms run their own certificate programmes now, and plenty of hiring managers genuinely respect them.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: I can see both sides. For someone mid-career who needs to reskill quickly, a micro-credential makes total sense — nobody's going to quit their job for a full degree. But for an eighteen-year-old, university offers much more than skills: networks, maturity, broader thinking.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Exactly. They're a supplement, not a replacement. I'd want proper national accreditation before treating one as equal to a degree.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Fair enough. If universities let you stack them into real qualifications, that solves the standards problem.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should university exams be handwritten or typed?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The discussion covered whether exams should be handwritten or typed. Speaker A supported handwriting, citing research that it aids memory and organisation of ideas, and warned that laptops risk crashes and pre-written answers. Speaker B argued that typing is fairer for fast thinkers with poor handwriting, matches the modern workplace, and makes marking and plagiarism checks easier. Speaker C proposed offering both formats, eventually suggesting typed exams as the default with handwritten on request. Overall, the group leaned towards typed exams with flexibility.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I actually support handwritten exams. Research shows writing by hand helps you remember and organise ideas. When I type, I just transcribe my notes without thinking, but handwriting forces me to process.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That might be true for note-taking, but exams are different. I think much faster than I can write, and my handwriting is terrible. Why should my grade suffer because my letters are messy? Typing is fairer, and it's what we'll use in every job.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But laptops bring their own problems — battery failures, software crashes, and the temptation to memorise and paste pre-written answers.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Couldn't we have both? Let students choose. Some people genuinely think better with a pen, others with a keyboard. The university could offer identical exams in both formats.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Choice sounds nice, but marking would be inconsistent. Typed exams are easier to mark fairly and you can run them through plagiarism software.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: True. Maybe typed should be the default, with handwritten available for anyone who requests it in advance.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Climate change is lengthening droughts across many agricultural regions, and plant scientists are racing to develop crops that can survive with far less water. Traditional breeding has already produced maize and sorghum varieties that maintain yields during dry seasons, while gene-editing techniques now allow researchers to adjust the roots, leaves and water-storage systems of plants with remarkable precision. Some modified crops close the pores on their leaves more quickly during heat, losing less moisture to the air. Critics caution that drought-tolerant seeds can be expensive, and that small farmers may become dependent on a handful of biotechnology companies. Supporters reply that public research institutes are developing open-access varieties, and that without such innovations, harvests in the driest regions will fail more often, pushing millions deeper into hunger.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: As climate change lengthens droughts, scientists are using traditional breeding and gene editing to create crops that need less water, though critics worry about costly seeds and corporate dependence, while supporters argue that public research and open-access varieties are essential to protect harvests in the driest regions.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Online reviews shape what billions of consumers buy, yet their reliability is increasingly in doubt. Studies estimate that a significant share of reviews on major platforms are fake, written by bots, paid freelancers or the sellers themselves. Even genuine reviews can mislead: people are far more likely to post after extreme experiences, so products receive disproportionately glowing or furious ratings. Platforms have responded with verification badges, purchase confirmation and algorithms that detect suspicious posting patterns, but determined manipulators adapt quickly. Researchers advise readers to ignore the average score and instead read the three-star reviews, which tend to describe both strengths and weaknesses, and to look for detailed comments mentioning specific features rather than emotional one-line judgments, which are often the least trustworthy of all.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although online reviews guide billions of purchases, many are fake or biased towards extreme experiences, and while platforms fight manipulation with verification and algorithms, researchers recommend reading detailed three-star reviews rather than trusting average scores or emotional one-line judgments.

essay.prompt: Some people think universities should prepare students for specific careers, while others believe university education should focus on developing broad knowledge and thinking skills. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.

(2) Arguments for career preparation: high tuition fees demand a return on investment, employers want job-ready graduates, economies face skills shortages in technical fields. (3) Arguments for broad knowledge: jobs change rapidly so transferable thinking skills last longer, universities serve society beyond the labour market, narrow training becomes outdated quickly. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. degrees should combine a broad intellectual core with practical options and internships. Useful phrases: 'Proponents of career-focused education argue that…', 'While it is true that…', 'A further consideration is…', 'Taking both views into account, I am inclined to believe…'

summarizeSpokenText.title: Wind turbines and wildlife
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture discussed how wind turbines affect birds and bats. The speaker said the problem is often exaggerated, since buildings, domestic cats and power lines each kill far more birds than turbines do, though the effect still matters for rare, slow-breeding birds of prey. Solutions include painting one blade black, which reduced collisions by over seventy percent in Norwegian trials, and radar systems that pause turbines when migrating flocks approach. The speaker concluded that careful siting and simple design changes let wind energy and wildlife protection advance together.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Wind power is essential to decarbonising electricity, but spinning turbines kill birds and bats. The scale of the problem is often misunderstood. Studies suggest that buildings, domestic cats and power lines each kill far more birds than turbines do. Nevertheless, the effect matters for rare species, particularly birds of prey. Solutions are emerging. Painting one turbine blade black reduces collisions by over seventy percent in Norwegian trials, because the blades become visible. Radar systems can pause turbines when migrating flocks approach. The lesson is that thoughtful siting and simple design changes let wind energy and wildlife protection advance together.

summarizeSpokenText.title: The growth of electric ferries
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture described the growth of electric ferries in Norway, where more than sixty now operate. The speaker listed the advantages: zero local emissions, far less noise, and running costs roughly eighty percent lower than diesel, with batteries recharged at the dock in about ten minutes. The technology suits short, fixed routes, but ocean crossings remain impossible with current batteries, so shipbuilders are testing hybrids and hydrogen fuel cells. Analysts predict most new ferries will be fully electric within a decade.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Norway's fjords have become a testing ground for electric shipping. The country's first battery-powered ferry entered service in 2015, and today more than sixty electric ferries cross Norwegian waters. The advantages are considerable: zero local emissions, far less noise, and running costs roughly eighty percent lower than diesel. Batteries are recharged at the dock during loading, a process that takes about ten minutes. The technology suits short, fixed routes perfectly, but ocean crossings remain impossible with current batteries. Shipbuilders are therefore experimenting with hybrid systems and, for longer routes, hydrogen fuel cells. Industry analysts predict that within a decade, most new commuter and car ferries worldwide will be fully electric.
